screens.title: String, StringBuilder, StringBuffer
screens.subtitle: Why immutability matters, how to manipulate text, and when to use mutable builders

narration.text: In this lesson you'll build a clear mental model of Java text: what makes a String immutable, how that leads to the string literal pool, and why mutable builders exist. We'll connect the idea of immutability to thread-safety and to common mistakes like using the equals operator for content checks. You will also learn practical methods for trimming, splitting, searching, and replacing text, and you'll see when repeated concatenation becomes a performance problem. Finally, we will contrast StringBuilder and StringBuffer so you can pick the right tool: one avoids synchronization for speed, the other adds synchronization for safety in multi-threaded code. By the end you will be able to choose the correct A P I for building and comparing strings, and you will understand simple performance trade-offs that matter in real programs. A short hands-on task shows how to use StringBuilder to construct and mutate a message without creating many intermediate objects.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: String is immutable and thread-safe; use StringBuilder for efficient single-threaded mutation and StringBuffer when synchronization is required.

screens.title: String Immutability — What it means and why it matters
screens.subtitle: A String's contents never change; operations return new String objects

narration.text: Immutability means an object's state cannot change after it is created. In Java, a String is immutable: once you construct a String with particular characters, that object forever represents that sequence. Methods that look like they change a string—such as concat, replace, or substring—actually return a new String instance with the requested content while leaving the original untouched. This makes Strings inherently thread-safe: multiple threads can share a reference without needing locks because nobody can change the content. It also enables the JVM to optimize memory: identical string literals can be interned in a pool so references can be reused. A common performance implication is that repeated modifications, for example concatenating in a loop, create many short-lived String objects and increase GC pressure. A practical way to think about it is a locked box analogy: the String's content is in a sealed box; to produce modified content you build a new box. One clear misconception is thinking concat modifies the original; test with references to observe a new object is returned. Key takeaway: prefer immutable Strings for stable keys and text that rarely changes, and choose a mutable builder when you will perform many incremental changes.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: String is immutable; operations that appear to modify a string create new String objects.

content.html:
Core Concept
String Immutability
A String object cannot change after creation. Transformations produce new String objects, leaving originals intact.
Why it matters
Thread-safety, predictable behavior, and caching opportunities for hash codes and pools.
Common misconception
Calling concat or replace changes the original object — it doesn't. You get a new object instead.
Concrete example
If greeting = "Hello" and you call greeting.concat("!") the returned value is a new String. The original greeting still refers to "Hello".
Key Takeaway

Use String when content is fixed or used as map keys; avoid repeated modification with + in loops.

Illustration: new object creation
String a = "Hello";
String b = a.concat(" World");
// a still refers to "Hello"; b refers to a new String "Hello World"
Why immutability helps
  • Safe sharing across threads without synchronization.
  • Stable hash codes make Strings reliable map keys.
  • Literal interning reduces duplicate objects for identical text.
Watch out:
Heavy modification patterns should use a mutable builder to avoid unnecessary allocations.

screens.title: Common String methods — trim, substring, indexOf, replace, split
screens.subtitle: Practical examples and common return behaviors

narration.text: Knowing common String methods and their behavior is essential for everyday Java code. Methods like length, isEmpty, and isBlank let you check a string's size and whitespace quickly. trim removes leading and trailing whitespace while substring returns a new String for a portion of the original. indexOf and lastIndexOf locate characters or substrings and return -1 when not found. replace — whether replacing characters or substrings — returns a new String with the replacement applied. split produces an array of substrings based on a delimiter. A practical pattern is to trim user input, check for emptiness or blank content, then perform case-insensitive comparisons if needed. A critical pitfall is assuming these methods mutate the original; they do not. We'll walk through a short code snippet that demonstrates these operations on a sample greeting. As you practice, remember to handle edge cases such as substring bounds and split results when the delimiter is absent. Common String methods — trim, substring, indexOf, replace, split means string methods return new strings or arrays; guard against edge cases like absent substrings or empty results.. In practical terms, practical examples and common return behaviors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Method quick-reference
keyIdea.text: String methods return new Strings or arrays; guard against edge cases like absent substrings or empty results.

content.html:
Definition / Methods
Common String methods
A compact code walkthrough shows typical method use and expected results.
String greeting = "  Hello, Cohortia!  ";
String trimmed = greeting.trim();
int len = trimmed.length();
String first = trimmed.substring(0,5); // "Hello"
String rest = trimmed.substring(7);   // "Cohortia!"
boolean has = trimmed.contains("Cohortia");
int i = trimmed.indexOf('o');
String replaced = trimmed.replace('o','*');
String[] parts = "apple,banana,cherry".split(",");
Explanation
  • trim removes only the ends; middle whitespace remains.
  • substring creates a new String and throws if indices are invalid.
  • indexOf returns -1 when the element is missing; check before using the index.
  • replace returns a new String and supports char or CharSequence replacements.
  • split returns an array; be careful with empty tokens and regex special characters.
Concrete Example

From " Hello, Cohortia! ", trim() yields "Hello, Cohortia!" and substring(0,5) yields "Hello".

Common mistake:
Assuming split with "," always returns three items; user input may vary and produce fewer tokens.

screens.title: String equality — equals() vs == vs intern()
screens.subtitle: Reference equality versus content equality and how the string pool affects ==

narration.text: String comparison is a frequent source of bugs. The == operator tests whether two references point to the exact same object in memory; it does not compare textual content. By contrast, equals compares the characters inside two strings and returns true when content matches. The JVM creates a string literal pool where identical string literals can reference the same object; that is why two literal declarations with the same text often make == return true. However, when you create a String with new, you explicitly allocate a separate object on the heap and == will return false compared to the pooled literal, even though equals will return true. The intern method forces a string's content into the pool and returns the pooled reference; this is useful when you need canonical references but is rarely necessary for everyday code. A common exam-style example: s1 == s2 is true for identical literals, s1 == s3 is false if s3 is created with new, and s1 == s3. intern() becomes true. Misinterpreting == for content equality is a practical bug that can break conditionals and map lookups. Always prefer equals for content comparison and reserve intern for special canonicalization cases.

keyIdea.title: Comparison rule
keyIdea.text: Use equals for content equality; == only verifies whether two references point to the same object.

content.html:
Comparison
equals() vs == vs intern()
Understand what each comparison means and when the pool influences reference equality.
String s1 = "Java";
String s2 = "Java";
String s3 = new String("Java");
String s4 = s3.intern();
System.out.println(s1 == s2); // true
System.out.println(s1 == s3); // false
System.out.println(s1 == s4); // true
System.out.println(s3.equals(s1)); // true
Explanation & pitfalls
  • == compares references, not content; equals compares characters.
  • String literals may be pooled so two literal references can be identical.
  • new String(...) always creates a distinct object on the heap.
  • intern() returns a pooled reference for canonicalization but is rarely needed.
Misconception

Seeing true from == does not guarantee content equality in all cases; test with equals to be sure.

screens.title: Why concatenation in loops is expensive
screens.subtitle: Each + or concat can create a new String; repeated operations cause allocation overhead

narration.text: Concatenating strings with + inside a loop looks simple but can be costly. Since String is immutable, each concatenation produces a new String object that copies the previous contents and the new addition. In a loop this leads to repeated allocation and copying proportional to the sum of lengths processed so far, which can result in quadratic time behavior and heavy garbage creation. A concrete scenario: appending a small token 10,000 times by using += creates many intermediate strings and increases runtime dramatically. A better approach is to use a mutable buffer, like StringBuilder, which appends in place without creating new objects each time. The typical refactor wraps a loop around a StringBuilder, calls append for each token, and then calls toString once at the end. If initial capacity is roughly known, passing it to the builder improves performance further by avoiding internal resizing. One misconception is assuming the compiler always optimizes away the cost; while compilers can optimize simple compile-time concatenations, they do not fix runtime loops that perform many concatenations. The principle is: use builders for repeated mutation to avoid allocation overhead and reduce GC pressure.

keyIdea.title: Performance principle
keyIdea.text: Repeated concatenation with String creates many objects; prefer StringBuilder for loops to reduce allocations and copying.

content.html:
Performance
Cost of repeated concatenation
A simple process diagram explains how each + produces a new object and how builders avoid that cost.
Inefficient pattern
String s = "";
for (int i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {
  s += "Java"; // creates a new String each iteration
}
Efficient refactor
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {
  sb.append("Java");
}
String result = sb.toString();
Key Takeaway

Prefer StringBuilder in loops; initialize capacity when you can to avoid resizing.

Common mistake

Assuming the + operator will be optimized in all runtime cases; it won't for runtime loops.

screens.title: StringBuilder — mutable, non-synchronized, performant
screens.subtitle: APIs: append, insert, delete, toString and capacity tuning

narration.text: StringBuilder is a mutable sequence of characters designed for efficient modifications in single-threaded contexts. Unlike String, StringBuilder updates its internal buffer when you call methods like append, insert, delete, or replace. These operations modify the same object rather than allocating new ones, which is why appending repeatedly to a builder is far more efficient than concatenating Strings. You can pass an initial capacity to reduce internal resizing; otherwise the builder grows automatically. After constructing the final content, call toString to obtain an immutable String snapshot. A few practical notes: insert allows you to place text at any index, delete removes a range, and append supports many types including primitives because methods are overloaded. A misconception is thinking toString returns the builder itself; it returns a new String that contains the builder's current content. Use StringBuilder when you perform many in-place edits on text within a single thread, and remember to reserve capacity when you expect large results for the best performance. StringBuilder — mutable, non-synchronized, performant means mutable, fast for single-thread use; use append/insert/delete and call tostring once to get the final string.. In practical terms, apis: append, insert, delete, tostring and capacity tuning. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: StringBuilder summary
keyIdea.text: Mutable, fast for single-thread use; use append/insert/delete and call toString once to get the final String.

content.html:
Definition
StringBuilder basics
Mutable character buffer for efficient single-threaded concatenation and mutation.
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
sb.append("Hello");
sb.append(", ");
sb.append("World!");
sb.insert(6, "Java ");
sb.delete(0,5); // removes characters at range
String result = sb.toString();
Practical guidance
  • Prefer StringBuilder in loops and concatenation-heavy code in single-threaded contexts.
  • Set an initial capacity when you can to avoid repeated resizing and copying.
  • Call toString once to produce the immutable result; don't convert on every append.
Key Takeaway

StringBuilder modifies its buffer in place, avoiding the allocation cost of repeated String concatenation.

Misuse:
Using StringBuilder across threads without synchronization can lead to corrupted content.

screens.title: StringBuffer — thread-safety with synchronization
screens.subtitle: Synchronized operations make it safe for concurrent modifications at a cost

narration.text: StringBuffer provides the same mutable A P I as StringBuilder but with synchronization on its public methods, making it safe for use when multiple threads might manipulate the same buffer. Each mutating method acquires a lock so only one thread changes the internal sequence at a time. This prevents race conditions when several threads append or delete characters concurrently. The trade-off is performance: synchronization adds overhead, so StringBuffer tends to be slightly slower than StringBuilder in single-threaded contexts. Use StringBuffer when shared mutation is necessary and you cannot control synchronization externally. A common pattern is to prefer StringBuilder for single-threaded work and either synchronize externally or use StringBuffer only when you require built-in thread-safety. Remember that synchronization protects the buffer's internal state but does not address higher-level invariants in your program; you may still need additional coordination for correctness. In short, pick safety when you need safe concurrent mutation, and pick speed otherwise. StringBuffer — thread-safety with synchronization means stringbuffer is like stringbuilder but synchronized; choose it when multiple threads must safely modify the same buffer.. In practical terms, synchronized operations make it safe for concurrent modifications at a cost. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: StringBuffer summary
keyIdea.text: StringBuffer is like StringBuilder but synchronized; choose it when multiple threads must safely modify the same buffer.

content.html:
Comparison
StringBuffer
Synchronized mutable buffer suitable for multi-threaded scenarios where the same instance is shared.
StringBuffer sbuf = new StringBuffer(100);
sbuf.append("First part.");
sbuf.append(" Second part.");
// Methods are synchronized internally
String result = sbuf.toString();
When to choose
  • Use StringBuffer when multiple threads will call mutating methods on the same instance.
  • Prefer StringBuilder when working in a single thread or when you can manage synchronization yourself.
  • Be aware that synchronization reduces throughput; measure only if necessary.
Pro Tip

If only a small critical section needs protection, prefer external synchronization around a StringBuilder rather than using a fully synchronized buffer.

screens.title: Performance demo: String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer
screens.subtitle: Measure concatenation in a loop and interpret timings

narration.text: A clear way to internalize the performance difference is to measure concatenation with each A P I. The pattern in the source measures time for repeated concatenation of a small token using String with +=, then StringBuilder, then StringBuffer. The String approach repeatedly allocates new objects and tends to be slow and memory-heavy. StringBuilder performs the same work without recreating the buffer, which is much faster. StringBuffer is comparable to StringBuilder but slightly slower due to synchronization overhead. When designing tests, avoid printing the fully concatenated result during timing because input and output can dominate measurements. Instead, measure elapsed time around the loop and optionally check final length. Also consider initial capacity: constructing a builder with an estimated capacity avoids internal array growth and copies. The practical takeaway is to profile and choose the builder for heavy dynamic construction; use String for fixed or small concatenations and when immutability is desired. Performance demo: String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer means stringbuilder outperforms repeated string concatenation; stringbuffer trades some performance for built-in thread-safety.. In practical terms, measure concatenation in a loop and interpret timings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Measured outcome
keyIdea.text: StringBuilder outperforms repeated String concatenation; StringBuffer trades some performance for built-in thread-safety.

content.html:
Live Coding
Performance comparison snippet
// Timing pseudo-code inspired by chapter source
int iterations = 100000;
String base = "Java";

long start = System.nanoTime();
String s = "";
for (int i = 0; i < iterations; i++) {
  s += base; // inefficient
}
long timeString = System.nanoTime() - start;

start = System.nanoTime();
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = 0; i < iterations; i++) {
  sb.append(base);
}
long timeBuilder = System.nanoTime() - start;

start = System.nanoTime();
StringBuffer sbuf = new StringBuffer();
for (int i = 0; i < iterations; i++) {
  sbuf.append(base);
}
long timeBuffer = System.nanoTime() - start;

// Compare timeBuilder < timeBuffer << timeString typically
Interpretation
  • String concatenation in a loop creates many intermediate objects and is slow.
  • StringBuilder provides the best single-threaded performance.
  • StringBuffer is slower than StringBuilder due to synchronization overhead.
Practical note

Use builders for heavy concatenation. Measure with time blocks and avoid printing during the timed section.

screens.title: Activity: Dynamic Message Builder using StringBuilder
screens.subtitle: Construct, modify, and display messages without creating many intermediate Strings

narration.text: This activity guides you through building a dynamic message using StringBuilder so you see mutation in practice. You will collect first name, last name, and a favorite language, append parts of the message incrementally, insert the current year after the greeting, replace a phrase, and finally produce an uppercase snapshot. The core learning is to perform in-place edits and call toString only when you need the immutable result. The activity shows how insert accepts an index and how replace or delete can modify ranges. A common gotcha is computing indexes after modifications; inserting text changes subsequent indices, so compute or search for anchor points carefully. Also demonstrate printing the message before and after calling toString and before converting to uppercase so you understand that the builder was mutated in place. This hands-on practice reinforces why StringBuilder avoids lots of short-lived objects while still giving you a final String when required. Activity: Dynamic Message Builder using StringBuilder means use stringbuilder to append, insert, replace, and snapshot the final message efficiently.. In practical terms, construct, modify, and display messages without creating many intermediate strings. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Activity goal
keyIdea.text: Use StringBuilder to append, insert, replace, and snapshot the final message efficiently.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Dynamic Message Builder
Follow the template and fill in the TODOs to practice builder operations.
import java.util.Scanner;

public class MessageBuilder {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in);

    // TODO: read firstName, lastName, language

    // 1. Use StringBuilder to construct the initial message
    StringBuilder messageBuilder = new StringBuilder();
    // TODO: append "Hello, " then names and the phrase

    System.out.println("Initial message: " + messageBuilder.toString());

    // 2. Insert the current year after "Hello, "
    int currentYear = java.time.Year.now().getValue();
    // TODO: find index and insert " (YYYY) "

    // 3. Replace "favorite language" with "preferred coding tool"
    // TODO: find and replace the substring

    System.out.println("Modified message (before uppercase): " + messageBuilder.toString());

    // 4. Convert to uppercase and print final message (snapshot)
    String finalUpperCaseMessage = messageBuilder.toString().toUpperCase();
    System.out.println("Final uppercase message: " + finalUpperCaseMessage);

    scanner.close();
  }
}
Hints & checks
  • Find the comma index then add two to place the year after "Hello,".
  • Use indexOf to locate the phrase to replace before calling replace on the builder string or use manual delete/insert.
  • Call toString only when you need an immutable snapshot for printing or storage.
Check your understanding

After completing the code, verify the builder was mutated by printing before and after insertions, then confirm the uppercase snapshot is separate.

narration.text: Summarize and commit a few compact rules to memory. First: Strings are immutable; transforming a String returns a new object. Second: Use equals for content equality and avoid == unless you intentionally compare references or interned literals. Third: When you need many incremental modifications, use StringBuilder for single-threaded performance and StringBuffer when you require built-in synchronization. These three rules cover most practical decisions you will make when working with Java text. Keep in mind that immutability provides safety and predictable behavior but can be costly for repeated mutation, which is where builders shine. When in doubt, profile the code: if your text manipulation is critical in a loop or hot path, refactor to a builder and measure the improvement. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: Keep a short checklist handy when coding: prefer String for fixed text and map keys because immutability ensures stable hashing; always compare text with equals, not ==; use StringBuilder to build strings in tight loops and avoid excessive allocation; use StringBuffer when you must have built-in synchronization for concurrent mutation. For exams and code reviews, these four quick rules answer most practical questions about Java text APIs. Finally, when you refactor, measure performance impacts and consider initial buffer sizing to avoid unnecessary reallocation. Asking yourself whether the code is single-threaded and whether you need to preserve original Strings will guide the correct A P I choice. Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Final Reminders
Use Strings as keys
Immutable Strings make reliable keys for maps and sets.
Avoid == for content
Always use equals or equalsIgnoreCase for text equality.
Prefer builders for loops
StringBuilder for speed; StringBuffer when you need synchronized mutation.
Final takeaway

Decide between immutability and mutation by asking: will this text change often? Will multiple threads touch it? Use that to choose String, StringBuilder, or StringBuffer.
